newsitem.title: INDIA: Mother Teresa's order looks to new leader.
newsitem.headline: Mother Teresa's order looks to new leader.

text.p: The Missionaries of Charity has revolved around Mother Teresa's iron-willed personality since she founded the Roman Catholic order nearly half a century ago.
Now the order's senior nuns have done what they had twice balked at doing -- elevated someone to succeed the Nobel Peace Prize winner.

The election of Sister Nirmala as superior general marks a watershed in the order's history and raises the question of whether Missionaries of Charity will continue to thrive without Mother Teresa's charismatic leadership.
Sister Nirmala was set to take over as the order's administrative leader on Friday, although her predecessor would continue to be called Mother, Missionaries of Charity said.

Last year, the Missionaries of Charity fed more than half a million people in some 111 countries. It teaches some 20,000 children in its schools and treats 90,000 lepers in its clinics. It also runs orphanages and homes for the dying.

The order includes approximately 4,500 nuns around the world who live a life of personal deprivation. The only worldly possessions they are allowed are three saris, a spoon and a plastic dish. They sleep on the floor.
Hundreds more volunteers queue up for lives of hardship in the order.
Mother Teresa, who has suffered from serious heart, kidney and lung ailments in recent years, never groomed a successor.
Usually the order's General Chapter holds a secret ballot among about 50 representatives of the nuns every five years.
Since 1950, these polls were a mere formality for Mother Teresa, who each time won undisputed support. This time she blessed Sister Nirmala after the 63-year-old nun was "almost unanimously" elected.
The chapter, which protects the order's constitution, had planned to meet last October to elect a superior general but the gathering was put off due to Mother Teresa's ill health.
More than 100 nuns from around the world went into retreat on January 16 and had expected to vote in a secret ballot on February 2.
But the order's electoral college, apparently unable to find a clear-cut successor, decided instead to hold closed-door deliberations before taking a vote.
The Vatican, which has no direct influence on the vote, must ratify the final choice.
Twice in the past the order had refused to agree to Mother Teresa's wish to step down. In past elections Mother Teresa had won all the votes -- except her own.
But as Mother Teresa's health began to deteriorate, insiders said they doubted she could take the strain.
In 1989, Mother Teresa was fitted with a pacemaker. In 1993, she broke three ribs in a fall and developed malaria.
She entered hospital in Calcutta last November with an irregular heart beat and suffered a series of heart failures. It was the third time since August she had been admitted for emergency care.

Until last September, sisters at the charity would not discuss the succession issue. "We will depend on prayers," one said. Sister Nirmala was considered a long-shot to succeed Mother Teresa. Three of the order's councillors-general had been favoured in the eight-week election process.
